title: "Session 0: From sequencing reads to community data"
---

```{r chunk-options, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = TRUE,
  error = FALSE,
  cache = FALSE,
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 5,
  fig.align = "center"
)
```

## What this session produces

This session starts with an ASV read-count table, taxonomic assignments,
a laboratory-to-field lookup, and sample metadata.

We will:

1. Connect sequencing records to their taxonomic and sampling information.
2. Inspect the process controls.
3. Apply confidence, control-count, and relative-frequency filters.
4. Construct community matrices and align their metadata.
5. Explore sequencing depth and sample accumulation.

The final outputs are a filtered read-count matrix, presence–absence and
relative-frequency matrices, and matching sample metadata.

<!-- Author note: Introduce the study, marker, sampling design, and the
relationship between a field site, a soil sample, a laboratory sample,
and an ASV. Explain what the four habitat categories represent. -->

## 1. Prepare the working environment

Open the tutorial repository as an RStudio Project. Save this document
as `session0.Rmd` in the repository's top-level directory.

Install the required packages once, if they are not already available:

```{r install-packages, eval=FALSE}
install.packages(
  c("here", "tidyverse", "janitor", "vegan", "iNEXT")
)
```

Load the packages for this session.

```{r packages}
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(vegan)
library(iNEXT)

# Declare this document's location relative to the project root.
here::i_am("session0.Rmd")

if (packageVersion("dplyr") < "1.1.1") {
  stop("Update dplyr to use the join checks in this tutorial.")
}
```

### Analysis settings

Keeping the main settings together makes it easier to explore how
different filtering decisions affect the results.

The values below reproduce the thresholds in the original workflow.
They are choices for this dataset rather than universal defaults.

```{r analysis-settings}
tax_ranks <- c(
  "species", "genus", "family", "order",
  "class", "phylum", "kingdom"
)

habitat_levels <- c(
  "heath", "regen", "com_wood", "mat_wood"
)

confidence_cutoff <- 0.7
relative_cutoff <- 0.001
min_reads <- 3000

positive_control_taxon <- "Mesembrina_mystacea"

# Use TRUE only for the original, uncorrected sample labels.
apply_label_correction <- TRUE

data_dir <- here::here("data", "session0")
```

<!-- Author note: Explain the classifier's confidence score and why these
thresholds were selected. Do not describe the score as a probability of
correct identification unless that interpretation is documented. -->

## 2. Read the four input tables

The tables describe different parts of the workflow. They are connected
through identifiers:

- `asv_id` connects read counts to taxonomy.
- `lab_id` connects sequencing columns to laboratory records and metadata.
- `sample_id` identifies the biological samples used in the analyses.

Check that the files are available before importing them.

```{r locate-inputs}
input_files <- c(
  counts = file.path(data_dir, "ASV_table.tsv"),
  taxonomy = file.path(data_dir, "ASV_tax_session0.csv"),
  lab_lookup = file.path(data_dir, "lab_field_id.csv"),
  metadata = file.path(data_dir, "CC_metadata_session0.csv")
)

missing_files <- input_files[!file.exists(input_files)]

if (length(missing_files) > 0) {
  stop(
    "Missing input files:\n",
    paste(missing_files, collapse = "\n")
  )
}
```

### ASV counts

The count table is initially wide: each laboratory sample occupies a
separate column.

```{r read-counts}
asv_tab <- read_tsv(
  input_files[["counts"]],
  col_types = cols(.default = col_character())
) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  mutate(
    asv_id = str_trim(asv_id),

    # Parse sample counts while preserving ASV identifiers as text.
    across(-asv_id, readr::parse_double)
  )
```

### Taxonomic assignments

This file contains the prepared rank hierarchy and assignment confidence
for each ASV. The taxonomic harmonisation that produced it is an upstream
preparation step.

```{r read-taxonomy}
asv_tax <- read_csv(
  input_files[["taxonomy"]],
  col_types = cols(
    .default = col_character(),
    confidence = col_double()
  )
) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  mutate(asv_id = str_trim(asv_id))
```

### Laboratory-to-field lookup

The lookup connects laboratory identifiers to field records. We retain
only the columns required here.

```{r read-laboratory-lookup}
lab_field_id <- read_csv(
  input_files[["lab_lookup"]],
  col_types = cols(.default = col_character())
) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  rename(field_id_lab = field_id) %>%
  transmute(
    lab_id = str_to_upper(str_trim(lab_id)),
    field_id_lab = na_if(str_trim(field_id_lab), "")
  )
```

### Sample metadata

Keep the complete metadata table, including samples with no sequencing
results. This allows us to distinguish missing sequencing records from
samples removed by filtering.

```{r read-metadata}
metadata_cc <- read_csv(
  input_files[["metadata"]],
  col_types = cols(
    sample_id = col_character(),
    lab_id = col_character(),
    field_id = col_character()
  ),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  mutate(
    sample_id = str_trim(sample_id),
    lab_id = na_if(str_to_upper(str_trim(lab_id)), ""),
    treatment = factor(
      str_trim(treatment),
      levels = habitat_levels
    )
  )
```

<!-- Author note: Describe the metadata variables and their units.
Clarify whether multiple soil samples belong to the same field site. -->

### Check identifiers and counts

The joins below assume one taxonomy record per ASV and one metadata
record per biological sample. This version also assumes one laboratory
sample per biological sample.

If technical replicates are present, their aggregation needs an explicit
rule before using this workflow.

```{r validate-inputs}
stopifnot(
  all(tax_ranks %in% names(asv_tax)),
  "confidence" %in% names(asv_tax),

  !anyNA(asv_tab$asv_id),
  anyDuplicated(asv_tab$asv_id) == 0,

  !anyNA(asv_tax$asv_id),
  anyDuplicated(asv_tax$asv_id) == 0,

  !anyNA(lab_field_id$lab_id),
  anyDuplicated(lab_field_id$lab_id) == 0,

  !anyNA(metadata_cc$sample_id),
  anyDuplicated(metadata_cc$sample_id) == 0,

  !anyNA(metadata_cc$treatment),

  all(
    is.na(asv_tax$confidence) |
      between(asv_tax$confidence, 0, 1)
  )
)

# Missing laboratory IDs are allowed for unsequenced samples.
metadata_lab <- metadata_cc %>%
  filter(!is.na(lab_id))

stopifnot(
  anyDuplicated(metadata_lab$lab_id) == 0
)

count_values <- asv_tab %>%
  select(-asv_id) %>%
  as.matrix()

stopifnot(
  ncol(count_values) > 0,
  is.numeric(count_values),
  all(is.finite(count_values)),
  all(count_values >= 0),
  all(count_values == round(count_values))
)

# Identify count-table ASVs without matching taxonomy records.
missing_taxonomy <- asv_tab %>%
  select(asv_id) %>%
  anti_join(asv_tax, by = "asv_id")

n_matched <- sum(asv_tab$asv_id %in% asv_tax$asv_id)

# Stop if there is no identifier overlap at all.
if (n_matched == 0) {
  stop(
    "No ASV identifiers match between counts and taxonomy. ",
    "Check the input files and identifier formats."
  )
}

tibble(
  count_table_asvs = nrow(asv_tab),
  matched_asvs = n_matched,
  unmatched_asvs = nrow(missing_taxonomy)
) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

## 3. Define taxonomic labels and sample types

### Choose the most resolved available taxonomic label

An ASV may have a species assignment, a genus assignment, or only a
higher-rank assignment. We use the first available name, starting with
species and working towards kingdom.

Several ASVs can therefore share one taxonomic label. The resulting
community matrix will describe these labels rather than individual ASVs.

```{r taxonomic-labels}
asv_tax <- asv_tax %>%
  mutate(
    # Treat empty rank entries as missing before choosing a label.
    across(
      all_of(tax_ranks),
      ~ na_if(str_trim(.x), "")
    ),

    consensus_name = coalesce(
      species, genus, family, order,
      class, phylum, kingdom
    )
  )
```

<!-- Author note: Explain the implications of mixing taxonomic ranks.
A genus-level label should not be described as a species identification. -->

### Correct the documented laboratory-label shift

The original workflow contains two linked corrections:

- `PC03` becomes `AP845`.
- `NC03` becomes `PC03`.

These corrections apply to the count-table labels. Keep
`apply_label_correction = FALSE` if the supplied table has already been
corrected.

```{r sample-key}
sample_key <- tibble(
  lab_id_original = setdiff(names(asv_tab), "asv_id")
) %>%
  mutate(lab_id = str_to_upper(lab_id_original))

if (apply_label_correction) {
  sample_key <- sample_key %>%
    mutate(
      lab_id = case_when(
        lab_id == "PC03" ~ "AP845",
        lab_id == "NC03" ~ "PC03",
        TRUE ~ lab_id
      )
    )
}

# Stop if corrected columns would collapse onto the same laboratory ID.
if (anyDuplicated(sample_key$lab_id) > 0) {
  stop("The label correction creates duplicated laboratory IDs.")
}
```

Classify the laboratory samples before filtering their read counts.
This preserves an inventory of controls even when they have no reads
assigned to the target group.

```{r classify-samples}
sample_key <- sample_key %>%
  # Attach field labels to distinguish extraction controls.
  left_join(
    lab_field_id,
    by = "lab_id",
    relationship = "many-to-one"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    sample_type = case_when(
      str_detect(lab_id, "^PC") ~ "PCR positive",
      str_detect(lab_id, "^NC") ~ "PCR negative",
      str_detect(
        coalesce(field_id_lab, ""),
        regex("extraction|blank", ignore_case = TRUE)
      ) ~ "Extraction blank",
      TRUE ~ "Field sample"
    )
  )

unidentified_samples <- sample_key %>%
  filter(
    sample_type == "Field sample",
    is.na(field_id_lab)
  )

if (nrow(unidentified_samples) > 0) {
  stop(
    "Some apparent field samples lack a field label. ",
    "Complete the lookup before classifying them."
  )
}

if (!any(sample_key$sample_type != "Field sample")) {
  stop("No process controls were recognised in the count table.")
}

sample_key %>%
  count(sample_type, name = "n_laboratory_samples") %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

<!-- Author note: Explain the purpose of the positive, negative, and
extraction controls. If IDs are anonymised, preserve or replace the
information used to recognise these controls. -->

## 4. Reshape the counts and attach taxonomy

A long table gives each ASV–laboratory-sample combination its own row.
This structure makes it easier to join information and apply filters.

Zero counts are omitted from this long detection table. We will restore
zeros when constructing the community matrix.

```{r long-detection-table}
asv_long <- asv_tab %>%
  # Turn the laboratory-sample columns into identifier–count pairs.
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -asv_id,
    names_to = "lab_id_original",
    values_to = "reads"
  ) %>%
  filter(reads > 0) %>%

  # Attach corrected laboratory IDs and sample classifications.
  left_join(
    sample_key,
    by = "lab_id_original",
    relationship = "many-to-one"
  ) %>%

  # Attach one prepared taxonomy record to each ASV.
  left_join(
    asv_tax,
    by = "asv_id",
    relationship = "many-to-one"
  )
```

<!-- Author note: Explain why long data are useful for joins and filtering,
while matrix data are useful for community analyses. -->

## 5. Inspect the process controls

We first restrict the control records to Metazoa and combine ASVs that
share the same taxonomic assignment.

Control counts are assessed before the confidence filter, matching the
original workflow.

```{r aggregate-controls}
controls <- asv_long %>%
  filter(
    sample_type != "Field sample",
    kingdom == "Metazoa"
  ) %>%
  group_by(
    lab_id, sample_type, consensus_name,
    across(all_of(tax_ranks))
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    reads = sum(reads),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

### Visualise control detections

The heatmap compares taxonomic read counts across process controls.
For the displayed labels, missing control–label combinations are filled
with zero, including controls with no metazoan detections.

```{r control-heatmap, fig.height=7}
if (nrow(controls) > 0) {

  control_inventory <- sample_key %>%
    filter(sample_type != "Field sample") %>%
    select(lab_id, sample_type)

  control_counts <- controls %>%
    group_by(lab_id, sample_type, consensus_name) %>%
    summarise(reads = sum(reads), .groups = "drop")

  control_plot_data <- tidyr::expand_grid(
    control_inventory,
    consensus_name = sort(unique(controls$consensus_name))
  ) %>%
    left_join(
      control_counts,
      by = c("lab_id", "sample_type", "consensus_name"),
      relationship = "one-to-one"
    ) %>%
    mutate(reads = replace_na(reads, 0))

  ggplot(
    control_plot_data,
    aes(
      x = lab_id,
      y = fct_rev(factor(consensus_name)),
      fill = reads
    )
  ) +
    geom_tile(colour = "black") +
    scale_fill_gradientn(
      name = "Read counts",
      colours = c("white", "red", "black"),
      values = c(0, 0.1, 1),
      limits = c(0, NA)
    ) +
    facet_grid(
      . ~ sample_type,
      scales = "free_x",
      space = "free_x"
    ) +
    labs(
      x = "Process controls",
      y = "Taxonomic assignment"
    ) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(
      panel.grid = element_blank(),
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
      axis.text.y = element_text(face = "italic")
    )

} else {

  cat("No metazoan reads were detected in the recognised controls.")

}
```

<!-- Author note: Interpret the actual heatmap after rendering.
Identify the deliberately introduced positive-control taxon and discuss
other control detections without assuming every detection has the same
source. -->

### Define subtraction thresholds

For each full taxonomic rank profile, we take the largest count observed
in any process control. This count will be subtracted from the
corresponding field-sample count.

The deliberately introduced positive-control taxon is excluded from
these thresholds.

This is the filtering rule used in this dataset. It does not establish
that all contamination has been removed, and it does not account for
differences in sequencing depth between controls.

```{r control-thresholds}
control_thresholds <- controls %>%
  filter(consensus_name != positive_control_taxon) %>%
  group_by(across(all_of(tax_ranks))) %>%
  summarise(
    threshold = max(reads),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Excluding the positive-control taxon from the thresholds does not remove
its detections from field samples. That distinction is retained from the
original workflow.

## 6. Filter the field-sample detections

### Select the target group and confident assignments

Keep field samples assigned to Metazoa with a reported confidence score
at or above the chosen cutoff. Records with missing confidence scores
are not retained.

The `semi_join()` restricts the analysis to laboratory IDs represented
in the study metadata, without adding metadata columns at this stage.

```{r select-field-detections}
field_detections <- asv_long %>%
  filter(
    sample_type == "Field sample",
    kingdom == "Metazoa",
    confidence >= confidence_cutoff
  ) %>%
  semi_join(
    metadata_lab,
    by = "lab_id",
    na_matches = "never"
  )
```

### Combine ASVs with the same assignment

Counts are aggregated within each laboratory sample before applying the
taxonomic control threshold.

```{r aggregate-field-counts}
field_counts <- field_detections %>%
  group_by(
    lab_id, consensus_name,
    across(all_of(tax_ranks))
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    reads = sum(reads),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

### Subtract the control threshold

The join uses the full rank profile. Matching missing lower ranks is
intentional: an unresolved genus-level assignment can still match the
same genus-level profile in the controls.

Assignments absent from the control table receive a threshold of zero.

```{r subtract-control-counts}
field_corrected <- field_counts %>%
  left_join(
    control_thresholds,
    by = tax_ranks,
    na_matches = "na",
    relationship = "many-to-one"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    threshold = replace_na(threshold, 0),

    # Clamp corrected counts at zero before removing non-detections.
    reads = pmax(reads - threshold, 0)
  ) %>%
  filter(reads > 0)
```

### Remove low-frequency detections

Calculate each assignment's fraction of the remaining target-group
reads within its laboratory sample. Retain fractions strictly above
0.001, equivalent to 0.1%.

The denominator is the post-subtraction metazoan total, not the total
number of raw sequencing reads.

```{r relative-frequency-filter}
asv_clean <- field_corrected %>%
  group_by(lab_id) %>%
  mutate(relfreq = reads / sum(reads)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(relfreq > relative_cutoff) %>%

  # Recalculate totals after the low-frequency detections are removed.
  group_by(lab_id) %>%
  mutate(
    total_reads = sum(reads),
    relfreq = reads / total_reads
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```

<!-- Author note: Explain the intended role and limitations of each filter.
Distinguish a filtering decision from evidence that a taxon is absent
from the sampled environment. -->

## 7. Attach metadata and audit sample retention

Attach the study metadata using the laboratory identifier.

```{r attach-metadata}
asv_cc <- asv_clean %>%
  left_join(
    metadata_lab,
    by = "lab_id",
    relationship = "many-to-one"
  )

if (nrow(asv_cc) == 0) {
  stop("No field detections remain after filtering.")
}
```

### Separate missing sequencing records from filtering losses

Start the audit from the complete metadata table. This keeps samples
that are absent from the count table in the accounting.

An entry in the count table does not necessarily imply that reads
survived the filters.

```{r first-retention-audit}
sample_audit <- metadata_cc %>%
  mutate(
    in_count_table = lab_id %in% sample_key$lab_id,
    has_filtered_detections = sample_id %in% asv_cc$sample_id,

    status_before_depth = case_when(
      !in_count_table ~ "Absent from count table",
      !has_filtered_detections ~ "No detections after filtering",
      TRUE ~ "Retained before depth filter"
    )
  )

sample_audit %>%
  count(treatment, status_before_depth, name = "n_samples") %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

Store the individual excluded records for local inspection. The object
is created without displaying identifying metadata in the tutorial.

```{r excluded-records}
excluded_first_stage <- sample_audit %>%
  filter(!has_filtered_detections) %>%
  select(
    sample_id, lab_id, treatment,
    in_count_table, status_before_depth
  )
```

<!-- Author note: Explain the observed pattern of sample loss across
habitats. Avoid interpreting samples with no retained detections as
confirmed biological absences. -->

## 8. Construct the community matrix

Community analyses generally use a matrix with samples in rows and taxa
in columns.

Before constructing it, check that a taxonomic label does not refer to
conflicting rank profiles. Otherwise, widening by label would combine
those profiles silently.

```{r check-taxonomic-labels}
taxon_lookup <- asv_cc %>%
  select(consensus_name, all_of(tax_ranks)) %>%
  distinct()

if (anyDuplicated(taxon_lookup$consensus_name) > 0) {
  stop(
    "Some taxonomic labels have conflicting rank profiles. ",
    "Resolve these labels before constructing the matrix."
  )
}
```

Now widen the filtered detection table. A zero represents no retained
detection for that sample–label combination.

```{r community-matrix}
comm <- asv_cc %>%
  select(sample_id, consensus_name, reads) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = consensus_name,
    values_from = reads,
    values_fill = 0,
    values_fn = sum
  ) %>%
  column_to_rownames("sample_id") %>%
  as.matrix()

tibble(
  n_samples = nrow(comm),
  n_taxonomic_labels = ncol(comm)
) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

### Summarise filtered read depth

Read depth here is the number of reads remaining after the preceding
filters.

```{r filtered-read-depth}
read_depth <- asv_cc %>%
  distinct(sample_id, treatment, total_reads)

stopifnot(
  anyDuplicated(read_depth$sample_id) == 0
)

read_depth %>%
  summarise(
    mean_reads = mean(total_reads),
    min_reads = min(total_reads),
    max_reads = max(total_reads)
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

## 9. Explore read-based rarefaction

These curves describe the expected number of retained taxonomic labels
when taking smaller read subsamples from each filtered sample.

They are conditional on the preceding filtering and taxonomic
aggregation. They should not be interpreted as organism-based
rarefaction or as estimates of all species present.

Removing low-frequency detections can also change the curve shapes.
Warnings about missing singleton counts should therefore be examined
rather than automatically suppressed.

```{r calculate-rarefaction}
rarecurve_df <- vegan::rarecurve(
  comm,
  step = 100,
  label = FALSE,
  tidy = TRUE
) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(sample_id = as.character(Site)) %>%

  # Attach habitat information to each sample's curve.
  left_join(
    metadata_cc %>% select(sample_id, treatment),
    by = "sample_id",
    relationship = "many-to-one"
  )
```

The vertical line marks the proposed minimum filtered read depth.

```{r plot-rarefaction}
p_rare <- ggplot(
  rarecurve_df,
  aes(x = Sample, y = Species, group = sample_id)
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = min_reads,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "red"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ treatment) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    x = "Filtered sequencing depth (reads)",
    y = "Expected retained taxonomic labels"
  )

p_rare
```

For a closer view of the first 5,000 reads, run:

```{r zoom-rarefaction, eval=FALSE}
p_rare + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 5000))
```

<!-- Author note: Interpret the actual curves. Explain the evidence and
practical considerations behind the minimum-depth choice. A flattening
curve alone does not establish complete ecological sampling. -->

## 10. Apply the minimum read-depth rule

Retain samples with at least 3,000 filtered reads under the current
settings. Their counts remain unchanged: this step excludes shallow
samples without rarefying the retained samples to a common depth.

```{r depth-retention-summary}
read_depth %>%
  mutate(retained = total_reads >= min_reads) %>%
  count(treatment, retained, name = "n_samples") %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r retain-community-samples}
asv_final <- asv_cc %>%
  filter(total_reads >= min_reads)

comm_keep <- comm[
  rownames(comm) %in% asv_final$sample_id,
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

if (nrow(comm_keep) == 0) {
  stop("No samples meet the minimum filtered read depth.")
}

# Remove taxonomic labels with no detections in the retained samples.
comm_keep <- comm_keep[
  ,
  colSums(comm_keep) > 0,
  drop = FALSE
]
```

### Match the metadata order to the matrix

Having the same sample identifiers is not sufficient: their order must
also match.

```{r align-metadata}
metadata_keep <- metadata_cc %>%
  slice(match(rownames(comm_keep), sample_id))

stopifnot(
  identical(rownames(comm_keep), metadata_keep$sample_id)
)

taxon_lookup <- taxon_lookup %>%
  filter(consensus_name %in% colnames(comm_keep))
```

### Complete the sample audit

The final audit distinguishes four outcomes.

```{r final-retention-audit}
sample_audit <- sample_audit %>%
  left_join(
    read_depth %>% select(sample_id, total_reads),
    by = "sample_id",
    relationship = "one-to-one"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    retained = sample_id %in% rownames(comm_keep),

    status = case_when(
      !in_count_table ~ "Absent from count table",
      !has_filtered_detections ~ "No detections after filtering",
      total_reads < min_reads ~ "Below minimum read depth",
      TRUE ~ "Retained"
    )
  )

sample_audit %>%
  count(treatment, status, name = "n_samples") %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

<!-- Author note: Discuss the final sample numbers and whether filtering
has changed the balance of sampling among habitats or field sites. -->

## 11. Create alternative community representations

The read-count matrix retains the corrected sequencing counts.

A presence–absence matrix records whether a taxonomic label has a
retained detection. A relative-frequency matrix divides each row by its
total retained read count.

Read frequencies are not direct estimates of organism abundance.

```{r alternative-community-matrices}
comm_pa <- vegan::decostand(
  comm_keep,
  method = "pa"
)

comm_relfreq <- vegan::decostand(
  comm_keep,
  method = "total"
)

stopifnot(
  all(comm_pa %in% c(0, 1)),
  all(abs(rowSums(comm_relfreq) - 1) < 1e-8)
)
```

<!-- Author note: Explain which ecological questions each representation
can address, and which information is discarded by converting to
presence–absence. -->

## 12. Explore sample accumulation within habitats

Read-based rarefaction varies the number of reads within one sample.
Here we change the sampling unit: we accumulate soil samples within each
habitat.

For each habitat, iNEXT receives:

1. The total number of retained soil samples.
2. The number of those samples in which each taxonomic label was detected.

The detection frequencies come from the presence–absence matrix.

```{r prepare-incidence-frequencies}
samples_by_habitat <- split(
  metadata_keep$sample_id,
  metadata_keep$treatment,
  drop = TRUE
)

inext_input <- purrr::map(
  samples_by_habitat,
  function(sample_ids) {

    mat <- comm_pa[sample_ids, , drop = FALSE]

    # Count detections across samples for each taxonomic label.
    freq <- colSums(mat)
    freq <- freq[freq > 0]

    # iNEXT requires the sampling-unit count as the first entry.
    c(nrow(mat), freq)
  }
)

tibble(
  habitat = names(inext_input),
  n_samples = purrr::map_dbl(inext_input, ~ .x[1]),
  observed_labels = purrr::map_int(
    inext_input,
    ~ length(.x) - 1L
  )
) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

### Estimate richness accumulation

Setting `q = 0` selects taxon richness. The fixed seed makes the bootstrap
results reproducible for a given dataset and software environment.

```{r estimate-accumulation}
set.seed(123)

inext_results <- iNEXT::iNEXT(
  inext_input,
  q = 0,
  datatype = "incidence_freq",
  nboot = 100
)
```

```{r plot-accumulation}
iNEXT::ggiNEXT(inext_results, type = 1) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of soil samples",
    y = "Taxonomic-label richness",
    colour = "Habitat",
    fill = "Habitat"
  )
```

### Observed and estimated richness

The asymptotic estimates concern the retained taxonomic labels under the
sampling and detection process represented by these data.

```{r richness-estimates}
inext_results$AsyEst %>%
  filter(Diversity == "Species richness") %>%
  select(
    Assemblage, Observed, Estimator, LCL, UCL
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

Soil samples are accumulated individually. Where samples are clustered
within field sites, these standard confidence intervals do not account
for that clustering.

## 13. Save the prepared data for the next session

Save a dedicated Session 0 bundle rather than overwriting the original
multi-dataset RDS files.

The bundle contains the community matrices, aligned metadata, retained
taxonomy, sample audit, and filtering settings.

```{r save-session0-data}
session0_data <- list(
  comm = comm_keep,
  comm_pa = comm_pa,
  comm_relfreq = comm_relfreq,
  metadata = metadata_keep,
  taxonomy = taxon_lookup,
  sample_audit = sample_audit,

  settings = list(
    confidence_cutoff = confidence_cutoff,
    relative_cutoff = relative_cutoff,
    min_reads = min_reads,
    positive_control_taxon = positive_control_taxon,
    apply_label_correction = apply_label_correction,
    habitat_levels = habitat_levels
  ),

  session_info = utils::sessionInfo()
)

derived_dir <- here::here("data", "derived")

dir.create(
  derived_dir,
  recursive = TRUE,
  showWarnings = FALSE
)

saveRDS(
  session0_data,
  file.path(derived_dir, "session0_metazoa.rds")
)
```

This RDS contains real derived data and sample metadata. Keep it with
the private data unless a version has been approved for public release.
